\chapter{He, She, and the Polite You}
\label{ch:habla}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what someone else does, and address someone respectfully, with one form.}

One form doing three jobs, and the vuestra merced fossil behind it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[habla]{habla — \textquotedblleft{}he speaks,\textquotedblright{} and the polite \textquotedblleft{}you speak\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-habla}



\begin{quote}
Two forms so far. Which means \emph{I speak}? (\emph{Hablo}.) Which is \emph{you speak}, to a friend? (\emph{Hablas}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: take the -s away again}]
Drop the \textbf{-ar}, add just \textbf{-a}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{hablar} $\to$ \textbf{habla} — \emph{he speaks}, \emph{she speaks}.
\end{quote}

That is the third form, and the third ending: \textbf{-o}, \textbf{-as}, \textbf{-a}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same form does a second job}]
Back when you met \emph{usted}, you were told it takes the \emph{he/she} form of the verb. Here is the first verb where you can actually see it happen.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{usted habla} — \emph{you speak}, politely.
\end{quote}

The same word, \textbf{habla}, covers \emph{he speaks}, \emph{she speaks}, \textbf{and} the respectful \emph{you speak}. Nothing extra to learn — it is one form doing three jobs, and that is a gift, not a complication.

Why? Because \emph{usted} was never a word for \emph{you} to begin with. It grew out of \emph{vuestra merced}, \textquotedblleft{}your grace\textquotedblright{} — and \emph{your grace} is a \textbf{thing you talk about}, not a person you talk to. You would say \textquotedblleft{}your grace \textbf{speaks},\textquotedblright{} not \textquotedblleft{}your grace speak.\textquotedblright{} The verb form is a fossil of that politeness.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin's ending here was \textbf{-at}: \emph{hablat}, \textquotedblleft{}he speaks.\textquotedblright{} Spanish let the final \textbf{-t} fall away, as it let most final consonants fall away, and the bare \textbf{-a} is what was left standing.

French did the same thing and went further — it writes \emph{parle} but the ending is now silent. Italian kept more: \emph{parla}. Three languages, one Latin ending, three degrees of wear.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habla\textquotedblright{}
  \item it for a friend's brother, then for a stranger you are being polite to — same word both times
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}he speaks\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Habla}.) Which form does \emph{usted} take, and why? (\textbf{Habla} — because \emph{usted} began as \emph{vuestra merced}, \textquotedblleft{}your grace,\textquotedblright{} something you talk \emph{about}.) What did Latin's \emph{-at} lose? (Its \textbf{-t}.) Next chapter is a review — no new words at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
